name: Tomas Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an apprentice lineworker, but I'm placed with the power company through a labour agency, so technically I work for the agency. We cover the hill villages above Kestrel, lots of forest, so most of our work is trees on lines after wind. I drag branches, set up the traffic signs, hand things up and sometimes climb with Henrik watching me like a hawk. I'm slower than the others at the rigging, still, but I'm getting there.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My placement gets reviewed every six months. The next review is in March, and there's talk the power company wants fewer agency people. I live with my girlfriend Petra, who does early shifts at the bakery, and we've got maybe a few weeks of rent put by. There's not much else round here except the quarry and the sawmill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, leave us alone. I don't use any of that AI stuff and I don't want to. I'd say it at the depot and people would mostly nod.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My worry was never about AI. It's the March review. If the power company cuts agency people, I'm out, and there's nothing else in the hills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up early and doing whatever Henrik asks, so they've got no reason to drop me. I'd stop eating out entirely and put off getting the car's tyres done. And I'd wait for March and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense. Like waiting for a phone call that might not come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at home if the March review goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have to move back in with my parents, in their spare room down in Kestrel. Petra would hate it. My dad would be fine with it, but he'd make comments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you thought about a backup, like the sawmill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sort of. The sawmill pays even less, and the quarry wants people with plant tickets I don't have. I'd ask, but I'm not counting on it.

say: I'd say **leave us alone**; I don't use AI and don't want to.
I'd say it at the **depot**, where people would mostly nod.
think: I think my real worry is the **March review** of my agency placement.
I think if they cut agency people, there's **nothing else** in the hills.
do: I'd turn up **early** and do whatever my trainer asks.
I'd stop **eating out** and delay the car's tyres while waiting for March.
feel: I'd feel **tense**, like waiting for a phone call.
S0.quote: My worry was never about AI. It's the March review. If the power company cuts agency people, I'm out, and there's nothing else in the hills.
fieldNote: He's already **anxious** before AI: his agency placement is reviewed in March.
His fallback is **moving back** in with his parents, which strains his relationship.
He has **few local options**: the sawmill pays less and the quarry needs tickets he lacks.

steps.text: Turn up early every shift before the March placement review
Stop eating out and delay replacing the car tyres
Wait for the March review before deciding anything else

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine for office people, not for us. You can't trim a tree off a line with a computer. That's what I'd tell anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company uses software for planning and maps the trees from satellites, they'll need fewer people out walking lines. That's some of what agency people do. I'd be the first to go, because I'm the cheapest to drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down, do the work and learn the new app only if they make me. I'd cut back harder, no takeaways, no nights out, and ask my dad if we could come back for a bit if it all went wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be counting days to the next review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the app only if forced. Who would force you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Henrik, probably. He'd say learn it or you're off the crew. He's not mean, he just tells you how it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you blame anyone for this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Nobody's evil here. The company wants to save money, the government wants cheap power. I'm just at the bottom of the pile.

say: I'd say it's fine for **office people**, not for us.
I'd say you can't **trim a tree** off a line with a computer.
think: I think satellite **tree mapping** means fewer people walking lines.
I think I'm the **cheapest to drop** as an agency apprentice.
do: I'd learn the **new app** only if forced.
I'd cut **takeaways** and ask my dad about moving back if needed.
feel: I'd feel **anxious**, counting days to the next **review**.
S1.quote: Nobody's evil here. The company wants to save money, the government wants cheap power. I'm just at the bottom of the pile.
fieldNote: He blames **no one**, a centrist view of a system where he's simply lowest.
He sees **satellite mapping** of trees cutting the line-walking that agency staff do.
He'd learn new tech **only under orders**, consistent with his resistance.

steps.text: Learn the company's job app only when Henrik requires it
Cut takeaways and nights out to save rent money
Ask his dad about moving into the spare room in Kestrel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and somebody should slow it down. I'm not a political person, but even I'd want the government to do something. People round here would be scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, in two years the planning goes to computers, and then by 2031 robots can do the climbing. I'm the agency apprentice. I'd be gone well before 2031, I reckon, because they'd stop renewing people like me as soon as they saw it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the quarry what tickets I'd need and maybe try to get one, even though I hate courses. I'd stop spending on anything except rent and food. If it all went, we'd move in with my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. I don't sleep well already before reviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 32 when the robots come. What would you look for then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with my hands that a robot wouldn't bother with, I don't know what. Maybe care work, like my mum did. I really don't have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Petra about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we might need to live with my parents for a while. My girlfriend Petra's bakery is already looking at a bread machine. That's two jobs at risk in one flat.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and somebody should slow it down.
I'd want the **government** to do something, though I'm not political.
think: I think the **agency** would stop renewing me well before robots arrive in 2031.
I think planning goes to **computers** first, and that's enough to cut me.
do: I'd ask the **quarry** what tickets I'd need and try for one.
I'd cut spending to **rent and food** and move in with my parents if needed.
feel: I'd feel **scared** and would lose **sleep**, as I already do before reviews.
S2.quote: My girlfriend Petra's bakery is already looking at a bread machine. That's two jobs at risk in one flat.
fieldNote: He expects to lose his placement **before robots** even arrive, because agency workers are dropped first.
His household has **two exposed jobs**: his and his girlfriend's bakery shifts.
He admits he has **no plan** beyond moving back home.

steps.text: Ask the quarry which plant tickets he'd need
Cut household spending to rent and food only
Move into his parents' spare room in Kestrel if the placement ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's still time for the government to sort out the rules. I'd want them to make sure people like me don't get dropped without warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd maybe get a direct job with the power company by then, if I'm lucky, but agency people would still go first. Even if I'm qualified by 2031, the robots come in 2034, and I'd only be a few years in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the power company every six months about a direct contract, and finish the apprenticeship if they let me. I'd save what I could, even if it's tiny. And I'd hold off on big decisions until I see how things go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still frightened, just slower. Five years is the same cliff, just further away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. Does that give you time to get off the agency?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Possibly. If the power company offered one, I'd do it. But I'd want someone to show me in person, not on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you hate courses. Would you actually do one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it if it meant keeping the job. I'm stubborn, not stupid.

say: I'd say there's **still time** for the government to sort the rules.
I'd want rules so workers aren't **dropped without warning**.
think: I think **agency people** would still go first, even with five years.
I think I'd only be **a few years in** when robots arrive in 2034.
do: I'd ask every six months for a **direct contract** with the power company.
I'd **save** what I could and hold off big decisions.
feel: I'd feel **frightened**, like the same **cliff**, just further away.
S3.quote: Five years is the same cliff, just further away.
fieldNote: He sees five years as only **delaying** the same outcome.
His one concrete goal is a **direct contract**, out of the agency.
He'd retrain **only in person** and only to keep the job: stubborn, not stupid.

steps.text: Ask the power company for a direct contract at every review
Save whatever is left after rent each month
Hold off on big decisions until the robot timeline is clearer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fine, there's time to sort it out. I wouldn't be shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, I'd still be worried, because I'd be 37 when the robots come, and I don't know anything else. But I'd have a decade to get settled and maybe find something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship, keep trying for a direct job, and save. If I got settled, I'd maybe do a plant ticket on the side so the quarry's an option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not like the others. I'd sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Would you still be on the lines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if they keep me. I'd want to be a full lineworker by then, not an agency apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Petra do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd maybe think about getting married. But we'd want some savings first. I don't want to start a family on nothing.

say: I'd say ten years is **fine** and there's time to sort it out.
think: I think I'd still be **worried** at 37, knowing nothing else.
I think a decade gives me time to **get settled**.
do: I'd finish the apprenticeship and keep trying for a **direct job**.
I'd maybe do a **plant ticket** on the side for the quarry.
S4.quote: I'd be 37 when the robots come, and I don't know anything else.
fieldNote: He'd sleep better, but still expects to **lose the line job** around 37.
The **agency contract** remains his first pressure, so mood stays anxious.

steps.text: Finish the apprenticeship and keep applying for a direct job
Take a plant ticket course so quarry work is an option
Put off a wedding until there are some savings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be gone before anyone figured out what to do. What would help is getting off the agency and onto a proper contract, so I'm not the first one dropped. And some help to get a plant ticket, so the quarry's a real option.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the agency thing. Half the young people on the power lines round here are agency workers, and nobody talks about us. We'd be the first to go in any of your pictures.

headlineQuote: Half the young people on the power lines round here are agency workers, and nobody talks about us.
portrait: Tomas is an **agency apprentice** placed with the power company in forested hill villages.
He lives with his girlfriend Petra, a bakery worker, and has **a few weeks** of rent saved.
His placement review in **March** worries him more than AI does.
He's **centrist**, blames no one, and avoids new tech unless ordered.
He's anxious even in AI Plateau and **alarmed** under both faster AGI pictures.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because as an **agency worker** he'd be dropped first.
whatWouldHelp: A **direct contract** with the power company.
Help getting a **plant ticket** so quarry work becomes an option.
